mainEntity.name: Is waist-to-hip ratio better than BMI?

acceptedAnswer.text: They measure different things — BMI reflects overall weight relative to height, while WHR reflects fat distribution. Many health professionals consider them complementary rather than one replacing the other.

mainEntity.name: Why do risk thresholds differ between men and women?

acceptedAnswer.text: Natural body fat distribution differs by sex on average, so WHO sets separate thresholds: a WHR of 0.90 or more for men and 0.85 or more for women indicates substantially increased risk.

mainEntity.name: What is a healthy waist-to-hip ratio?

acceptedAnswer.text: Using the WHO cut-offs, a ratio below 0.90 for men or below 0.85 for women is below the level linked to substantially increased risk of metabolic complications.

mainEntity.name: Should I use waist-to-hip or waist-to-height ratio?

acceptedAnswer.text: Both describe fat around the middle. Waist-to-height ratio needs only one tape measurement and is recommended by NICE in the UK; waist-to-hip ratio is the measure used in the WHO report. Checking both, alongside BMI, gives a fuller picture.
